title: Writing Good Prompts
about: Ask AI for what you want with a clear goal, context and format.

cards.prompt: What you type to a chatbot is called a **prompt**. A clear prompt says exactly what it wants, and what shape the answer should be. Is each prompt **vague** or **clear**?

items.label: Tell me all about rivers, please!

cards.hint: For each one, ask: does it say exactly what it wants, and how long or what shape?
cards.nudge: A long or polite prompt can still be vague. Look for the ones that say exactly what they want and what shape.
cards.explanation: The clear ones say the **goal** (explain, titles) and the **format** (3 sentences, 3 titles). "Help me with my email" doesn't say what help. "Tell me all about rivers, please!" is polite, but still vague: all of what, and how long?

cards.title: What a good prompt says
cards.body:
A chatbot writes likely words to follow **your** text, so the more your prompt says, the better it aims. Say:

- **The goal:** what you want done.
- **The context:** who it's for, what you already have.
- **The format:** how long, what shape.

Ask "Tell me about dogs" when you wanted puppy tips? Enjoy 2,000 words on poodle history.

cards.prompt: These bits are from different prompts. Is each one the **goal**, the **context** or the **format**?
cards.hint: Goal = what you want done. Context = who it's for, or what you already know or have. Format = the shape or length of the answer.
cards.nudge: "For my little brother" changes who it's aimed at, and "I've already read chapter 1" is something you know. What kind of part are those?
cards.explanation: **Goals** say what to do (summarise, plan). **Context** says who it's for or what you already know (your little brother, chapter 1). **Format** is the shape (a rhyme, a table).

cards.prompt: Your prompt is: **"Write a summary of the water cycle."** It has a goal. What would improve it **most**?

options.text: Asking it to include lots of facts and examples
options.nudge: More facts makes it longer, not better aimed. Who is it for, and what shape should it be?

options.text: Asking it to check its facts before it answers
options.nudge: Asking doesn't make it check, and this still doesn't say who it's for or how long.

options.text: Saying please, and that it's really important
options.nudge: Politeness and urgency don't tell it who the summary is for, or how long.

options.text: Saying who it's for and how long it should be

cards.hint: Check it against the three parts of a good prompt. Which ones are missing?
cards.explanation: It has a **goal**, but no **context** (who's it for? a 12-year-old? a science test?) and no **format** (one paragraph? five bullet points?). More facts, asking it to check itself, or saying it's important don't add either.

cards.prompt: You're giving a 1-minute talk about octopuses at your nature club.

steps.text: You type "octopus facts". The chatbot replies with 20 long paragraphs. What do you change?

choices.consequence: You get another 20 paragraphs, a bit different. Nothing you said changed, so nothing useful changed.

choices.text: "3 surprising octopus facts for a 1-minute talk, one sentence each"
choices.consequence: Much better: three short, surprising facts. One says an octopus has "nine brains".

choices.text: Turn the temperature right up for more interesting facts
choices.consequence: The facts get stranger, and some make no sense. Temperature changes how it picks, not what it knows.

steps.text: "Nine brains" sounds amazing. What do you do before using it?

choices.text: Check it on a trusted science website
choices.consequence: It's close: an octopus has one central brain plus a cluster of nerve cells in each of its 8 arms, so you say that.

choices.text: Use it: it's from a good prompt
choices.consequence: A good prompt gets a better-aimed answer, not a checked one. Surprising facts are exactly the ones to check.

cards.hint: Which parts of a good prompt was "octopus facts" missing? And does a better prompt make the answer checked?
cards.explanation: Saying the **goal, context and format** turned 20 paragraphs into 3 useful facts. But a good prompt doesn't make facts true: surprising ones still need **checking** in a trusted source.

cards.prompt: You can paste in what you have, like notes to summarise or a draft to improve. But keep private details out: chats may be stored, and you can't always take them back. Should each thing go **in** your prompt, or be **left out**?

items.label: How long the answer should be
Your home address, for a local answer
Your email password, to sort your inbox
A friend's private message to you

cards.hint: Ask of each one: does it help the chatbot aim the answer, and is it safe and mine to share?
cards.nudge: Some of these come with a helpful-sounding reason. Is the reason worth sharing something private?
cards.explanation: Who it's for, how long and your own notes help it aim. Your address and password are private even with a good reason (for a local answer, name your town or suburb instead), and a friend's private message isn't yours to share.

cards.prompt: "Give me facts about sharks" got a long, boring list. Which **one** change helps **most**?

options.text: "Give me lots of detailed, interesting facts about every kind of shark"
options.nudge: Longer and keener, but how many facts, what for, and how long each?

options.text: "Give me 3 surprising shark facts for a class talk, one sentence each"
"Give me shark facts. Be accurate, double-check them, make no mistakes"
options.nudge: Asking it to be accurate doesn't make it accurate, and it still doesn't say how many or what for.

options.text: "You are a shark expert. Tell me the most amazing facts about sharks"
options.nudge: That sets a style, but how many facts, for what, and how long?

cards.hint: Which parts of a good prompt was the original missing? Which option adds them?
cards.explanation: Only the 3-surprising-facts prompt says **how many** (3), **what kind** (surprising), **what for** (a class talk) and **what shape** (one sentence each). The others sound keen, careful or expert, but none says how many, what for, or how long.

cards.prompt: You want a chatbot to quiz you on your history notes.

steps.text: You paste your notes and type "Quiz me". It writes 10 questions, with the answers right underneath. The world's most generous quizmaster. What's the best fix?

choices.text: Cover the answers with your hand
choices.consequence: That works a bit, but it's easy to peek, and you didn't fix the prompt.

choices.text: "Ask me one question at a time. Don't show the answer until I reply"
choices.consequence: Now it asks, waits, and tells you if you were right. You said exactly what you wanted.
Harder questions, still with the answers underneath. The prompt didn't say what was wrong.

steps.text: Forty questions later, it starts showing the answers again. In a very long chat, a chatbot can lose track of the start. What do you do?

choices.text: Repeat your instruction: one question at a time, answers hidden
choices.consequence: It goes back to asking and waiting. Repeating the instruction put it back in front of the chatbot.
Easier questions, still with the answers. The problem was the lost instruction, not how hard the questions were.

choices.text: Keep going: it will remember the rule again soon
choices.consequence: The longer the chat gets, the further back your instruction is. It doesn't come back by itself.

cards.hint: What exactly went wrong with its answer each time? Say that in your next prompt.
cards.explanation: When an answer isn't what you wanted, **say what was wrong**: here, the format (one question at a time, answers hidden). In a very long chat it can lose track of the start, so **repeat your instructions**.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A good **prompt** says the **goal**, the **context** and the **format**.
- Paste in your notes or drafts, never private details.
- Long chat? It can lose the start, so repeat your instructions.

Next: checking AI's work.
